entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To say or do something that makes people who have just met feel more relaxed and comfortable talking to each other.
entries.usage: Common at parties, first dates, classes and the start of meetings; it is positive and neutral. The subject can be a person or the thing that helped (*The joke broke the ice*), and *to break the ice* often explains a purpose. The noun *icebreaker* means a game or question used for this.
examples: Nobody at the table knew each other, so I told a silly story about my flight to **break the ice**.
The teacher **broke the ice** on the first day by asking everyone about their worst haircut.
Our dogs started playing together, which **broke the ice** with our new neighbors.

drill.sentence: On our first date we were both nervous, but when I spilled coffee all over myself, it really {{broke the ice}}.
drill.hint: made us both feel relaxed with each other (not *lightened the mood*)

entries.related: *an icebreaker* — a game or question used to help people relax; *lighten the mood* — make a serious atmosphere less tense; *hit it off* — get along well right away.

entries.term: hit the nail on the head
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem, or to say something that is exactly right.
entries.usage: Informal and usually praise for someone else's comment: *You hit the nail on the head.* It is common in meetings and conversation, often in the past or present perfect. It is about describing or analyzing something correctly, not about doing a task well.
entries.pattern: you've hit the nail on the head; X hit the nail on the head (with + comment)
examples: When Maria said the real problem was the lack of parking, she **hit the nail on the head**.
Your review of the restaurant **hit the nail on the head**: great food, terrible service.
I think the doctor **hit the nail on the head** — my headaches started when I quit coffee.

drill.sentence: You've {{hit the nail on the head}} — the team doesn't lack talent, it lacks a real leader.
drill.hint: described the real cause exactly (a carpentry image; not *got it right*)

entries.related: *nail it* — informal, do or describe something perfectly; *spot on* — exactly right, more British; *miss the point* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The final problem in a series of problems, which makes a situation impossible to accept any longer.
entries.usage: Used when someone finally reacts strongly, quits or ends something: *That was the last straw.* Common patterns are *the last straw was when …* and *… was the last straw for me*. It implies many smaller problems came before; *the final straw* means the same.
entries.pattern: that was the last straw; X was the last straw (for someone)
examples: My roommate never cleaned up, and when he ate my birthday cake, that was **the last straw**.
For many riders, the third fare increase in two years was **the last straw**.
She'd put up with his lateness for months, but missing her mother's birthday dinner was **the last straw**.

drill.sentence: The landlord ignored the broken heater for weeks, and when the ceiling started leaking, that was {{the last straw}}; we moved out.
drill.hint: the one problem too many (the adjective is not *final*)

entries.related: *the final straw* — same; *the straw that broke the camel's back* — the full saying; *enough is enough* — said when you refuse to accept something any longer.
entries.origin: From the saying *the straw that broke the camel's back*: one light straw added to a very heavy load is finally too much.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something that seems bad or unlucky at first but later brings a good result.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and personal stories, usually said when looking back: *Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.* It often follows *turn out to be* or *was*. It sounds positive and a little reflective.
entries.pattern: X turned out to be / was a blessing in disguise
examples: Missing the flight turned out to be **a blessing in disguise** — I met my wife at the airport hotel.
Getting cut from the basketball team was **a blessing in disguise**; that's when I started playing guitar.
When the old hardware store closed, it was **a blessing in disguise** for the street: a busy bakery opened in its place.

drill.sentence: Breaking my leg was {{a blessing in disguise}}, because it forced me to slow down and finally write my novel.
drill.hint: a bad thing that turned out well (not *a silver lining*)

entries.related: *every cloud has a silver lining* — every bad situation has some good side; *a mixed blessing* — something with both good and bad sides; *a lucky break* — a piece of good luck.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Official rules, forms and procedures that seem unnecessary and make things slow and difficult.
entries.usage: Critical; common in news and complaints about government offices, insurance companies and permits. Typical verbs are *cut, cut through, reduce* and *deal with*. It is uncountable: *a lot of red tape*, never *red tapes*.
entries.pattern: cut (through) the red tape; a lot of / layers of red tape
examples: Opening a small café took eight months because of all the **red tape** at city hall.
It took weeks of **red tape** to get my mother's insurance to cover her wheelchair.
The county wants to cut the **red tape** for homeowners who build a small apartment over their garage.

drill.sentence: Getting a permit for a backyard fence shouldn't involve this much {{red tape}}.
drill.hint: slow official procedures (not *paperwork* or *bureaucracy*)

entries.related: *bureaucracy* — the system of officials and rules, more neutral; *paperwork* — the forms themselves; *jump through hoops* — do many difficult things to get something.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A practical rule based on experience rather than exact calculation, which works well enough in most cases.
entries.usage: Neutral and very common in advice about cooking, money, health and work. Typical frames are *As a rule of thumb, …* and *A good rule of thumb is to …*. It openly admits that the guideline is approximate, not exact.
entries.pattern: as a rule of thumb, …; a good rule of thumb is to …
examples: As **a rule of thumb**, leave a twenty percent tip at a sit-down restaurant.
A common **rule of thumb** says you should save three to six months of expenses for emergencies.
When I cook rice, my **rule of thumb** is two cups of water for every cup of rice.

drill.sentence: As {{a rule of thumb}}, you should replace your running shoes every three to five hundred miles.
drill.hint: a rough practical guideline (a body-part image)

entries.related: *a general rule* — similar, a bit more formal; *a ballpark figure* — a rough estimate; *by the book* — the opposite idea, following official rules exactly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deliberately ignore something wrong that you know is happening, instead of trying to stop it.
entries.usage: Usually critical; common in news and talk about authorities, employers and parents. The wrong thing follows *to*: *turn a blind eye to cheating*. It stresses a choice not to act, not a lack of knowledge.
entries.pattern: turn a blind eye (to + something)
examples: The manager **turned a blind eye** to staff taking long breaks, as long as the work got done.
For years, the city **turned a blind eye** to illegal parking outside the stadium.
My parents **turned a blind eye** when my brother came home late, but not when I did.

drill.sentence: The coach knew some of his players were skipping class, but he {{turned a blind eye}} as long as they kept winning.
drill.hint: deliberately ignored it (not *looked the other way*)

entries.related: *look the other way* — same, informal; *ignore* — plainer, not always deliberate; *crack down on* — the opposite, start dealing strictly with something.

entries.term: cost an arm and a leg
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be extremely expensive, often more than seems reasonable.
entries.usage: Informal and very common in conversation about prices: *That car must have cost an arm and a leg.* Besides *cost*, it works with *pay* and *charge* (*They charged us an arm and a leg*). It is a humorous exaggeration, so it doesn't fit formal writing.
entries.pattern: cost / pay / charge (someone) an arm and a leg
examples: Fixing the transmission is going to **cost an arm and a leg**, so we might just sell the car.
Daycare in this city **costs an arm and a leg**; it's more than our rent.
They paid **an arm and a leg** for front-row seats to the playoff game.

drill.sentence: I'd love to stay at that hotel by the beach, but it {{costs an arm and a leg}}.
drill.hint: is extremely expensive (a body image; not *a fortune*)

entries.related: *cost a fortune* — same, a little less informal; *break the bank* — cost more than you can afford, usually in the negative; *dirt cheap* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Feeling slightly ill or unwell, but not seriously sick.
entries.usage: Informal and polite; common when canceling plans or calling in sick: *I'm feeling a bit under the weather.* It usually follows *feel* or *be*, often with *a bit* or *a little*. It is vague on purpose, so it is not used for serious illness.
entries.pattern: feel / be (a bit / a little) under the weather
examples: I'm feeling a little **under the weather**, so I'm going to skip the gym tonight.
Our daughter has been **under the weather** all week, so we've stayed home.
The singer was clearly **under the weather**, but she still played the whole two-hour show.

drill.sentence: Sorry I didn't call back — I've been a bit {{under the weather}} since the weekend.
drill.hint: slightly sick (an idiom; not *unwell* or *run-down*)

entries.related: *run-down* — tired and weak, often before getting sick; *sick as a dog* — very sick, informal; *fit as a fiddle* — the opposite, very healthy.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To learn how to do something after some practice, so that it starts to feel easy.
entries.usage: Informal and very common about skills, tools and new jobs, often as encouragement: *Don't worry, you'll get the hang of it.* It is most often used with *it*. Frequent forms are *getting the hang of* and *once you get the hang of it*.
entries.pattern: get the hang of it / of + -ing; once you get the hang of it
examples: Driving a stick shift was scary at first, but I **got the hang of it** in about a week.
Don't worry about the new software — you'll **get the hang of it** after a few days.
My grandma is finally **getting the hang of** video calls; now she calls us every Sunday.

drill.sentence: Knitting seemed impossible at first, but once I {{got the hang of}} it, I made scarves for the whole family.
drill.hint: learned to do it well through practice (not *got used to* or *got the knack of*)

entries.related: *get the knack of* — similar; *learn the ropes* — learn the basics of a new job; *get used to* — become familiar with something, not necessarily skillful.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Over a long period of time, or in the end, after the short-term effects have passed.
entries.usage: Neutral and common in advice, money talk and decisions, usually in contrast with the short term: *It's cheaper in the long run.* It can go at the start or the end of a clause. *In the long term* is similar and a bit more formal.
examples: Good boots cost more now, but they save you money **in the long run**.
Moving closer to my parents was hard, but **in the long run** it was the right choice for the kids.
Cutting corners on safety might save time, but it'll hurt the company **in the long run**.

drill.sentence: Paying off your credit card every month is a pain, but {{in the long run}} you'll save a lot in interest.
drill.hint: when you look at the years ahead (not *over time* or *in the … term*)

entries.related: *in the long term* — similar, a bit more formal; *in the short run* — the opposite; *at the end of the day* — when everything is considered.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop working on something for the rest of the day, usually because you are tired or have done enough.
entries.usage: Informal and very common at work and on home projects, usually as a suggestion: *Let's call it a day.* It often follows *let's*, *I'm going to* or *I think we should*. *Call it a night* is used late in the evening, and *call it quits* means stop completely.
examples: We've been painting since eight this morning; let's **call it a day** and order pizza.
The coach **called it a day** after the rain turned the field into mud.
I'm exhausted, so I'm going to **call it a day** and finish the report tomorrow.

drill.sentence: It's four o'clock and nobody can think straight anymore — let's {{call it a day}}.
drill.hint: stop working for today (not *wrap up*; not the *quits* phrase)

entries.related: *call it a night* — same, late in the evening; *call it quits* — stop completely, often for good; *wrap up* — finish a task or meeting.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To avoid saying something directly or avoid getting to the main point, usually because it is uncomfortable.
entries.usage: Informal and mostly negative or a request: *Stop beating around the bush.* *I won't beat around the bush* is a common way to announce bad news or a direct question. *Around* is the American form; British English says *beat about the bush*.
examples: Stop **beating around the bush** and tell me what the doctor said.
I won't **beat around the bush**: we can't afford a vacation this year.
The salesman kept **beating around the bush** when I asked about the total price.

drill.sentence: My boss {{beat around the bush}} for ten minutes before admitting that the company was cutting my hours.
drill.hint: avoided getting to the point (not *hemmed and hawed*)

entries.related: *get to the point* — the opposite; *cut to the chase* — go straight to the important part; *hem and haw* — hesitate and avoid giving a clear answer.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To think in a creative, original way, instead of following the usual rules or ideas.
entries.usage: Very common in business, education and job ads; because it is used so much, many people now hear it as a cliché. It often appears as advice (*We need to think outside the box*) or praise. The adjective *outside-the-box* (*outside-the-box ideas*) is also common.
examples: With no money for ads, the shop owners had to **think outside the box**, so they started a cooking series online.
Good teachers **think outside the box** when a student just isn't getting it.
The firefighters had to **think outside the box** to get the horse out of the swimming pool.

drill.sentence: My grandpa really {{thinks outside the box}} — he turned an old bathtub into a vegetable garden.
drill.hint: has creative, unusual ideas (a shape image; not *gets creative*)

entries.related: *get creative* — informal, plainer; *think on your feet* — react quickly without preparing; *stick to the script* — the opposite, follow the usual plan.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Back at the starting point after an attempt has failed, so that you have to start again.
entries.usage: Informal and common at work and in daily life: *The deal fell through, so we're back to square one.* It sounds frustrated or resigned. Typical verbs are *be, go* and *send someone*.
entries.pattern: be / go back to square one; send someone back to square one
examples: The buyers backed out at the last minute, so we're **back to square one** with selling the house.
Our babysitter is moving to Ohio, so we're **back to square one**.
The test results came back normal, which sent the doctors **back to square one**.

drill.sentence: The bakery we booked for the wedding cake just closed, so we're {{back to square one}}.
drill.hint: at the very beginning again (not the *drawing board* phrase)

entries.related: *back to the drawing board* — start planning again after a plan fails; *start from scratch* — begin from nothing; *make headway* — the opposite, make progress.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To agree completely with someone, or to have exactly the same opinion about something.
entries.usage: Usually negative: *We don't always see eye to eye.* It is followed by *with* + person and *on* or *about* + topic. Because it softens a disagreement, it sounds polite and diplomatic.
entries.pattern: (not) see eye to eye (with someone) (on / about + topic)
examples: My sister and I don't **see eye to eye** on how to raise kids, so we avoid the topic.
The coach and the star player never really **saw eye to eye**, and he was traded after one season.
It took a while, but the neighbors finally **see eye to eye** about where the fence should go.

drill.sentence: My parents rarely {{see eye to eye}} on money; my mom saves everything and my dad loves to spend.
drill.hint: share the same view (not *are on the same page*)

entries.related: *be on the same page* — agree about how to do something, common at work; *agree to disagree* — accept that you won't agree; *be at odds* — the opposite, disagree.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Suddenly and without any warning, in a way you did not expect at all.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and stories about surprising calls, messages and events: *She called me out of the blue.* It usually goes after the verb, at the end of the clause, or at the start of the sentence. It can describe good or bad surprises.
examples: My college roommate texted me **out of the blue** after ten years of silence.
**Out of the blue**, the landlord told us we had to move out by the end of the month.
The storm seemed to come **out of the blue**; the forecast had promised sunny skies all weekend.

drill.sentence: We hadn't heard from my uncle in years, and then {{out of the blue}} he showed up at our door with a suitcase.
drill.hint: with no warning at all (a sky image; not *out of nowhere*)

entries.related: *out of nowhere* — same, informal; *a bolt from the blue* — a sudden shock; *all of a sudden* — suddenly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Strictly following the rules, the law or the official procedure.
entries.usage: It can be praise (careful, honest) or mild criticism (too rigid). It usually follows *do things*, *go* or *play it*: *She does everything by the book.* It is typical when talking about police, officials, managers and referees.
entries.pattern: do something / go / play it by the book
examples: Our new accountant does everything **by the book**, which is exactly what we need after last year's mess.
The officer went **by the book** and wrote me a ticket, even though I was only a few miles over the limit.
If you want the permit quickly, play it **by the book** and fill out every form.

drill.sentence: The referee called the game strictly {{by the book}}, so both coaches were annoyed by all the penalties.
drill.hint: following every official rule (a reading image)

entries.related: *play by the rules* — act fairly; *cut corners* — the opposite, skip steps to save time; *bend the rules* — break the rules a little.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To watch someone or something carefully, to make sure they are safe or that nothing goes wrong.
entries.usage: Neutral and extremely common in daily life: *Can you keep an eye on my bag?* It is used for children, pets, belongings, cooking, health and situations that might change. *Keep a close eye on* is stronger.
entries.pattern: keep an eye / a close eye on + someone / something
examples: Can you **keep an eye on** the kids while I run to the store?
**Keep an eye on** the rice; it burns if you don't stir it.
The doctors want to **keep an eye on** him overnight after the fall.

drill.sentence: Could you {{keep an eye on}} my laptop for a minute while I grab a coffee?
drill.hint: guard it for a moment (not *look after* or *watch*)

entries.related: *look after* — take care of; *keep tabs on* — follow closely what someone is doing; *lose sight of* — the opposite, stop paying attention.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To start a project, business or plan and make it begin working successfully.
entries.usage: Common in business and news, often with *help*, *try* or *struggle*: *We're trying to get the project off the ground.* The thing goes in the middle, and *never got off the ground* describes a plan that failed early. The image is a plane taking off: the start is the hardest part.
entries.pattern: get + project / business / plan + off the ground; never get off the ground
examples: It took her two years and a small bank loan to **get** the bakery **off the ground**.
The plan for a new community pool never **got off the ground** because nobody could agree on the location.
A few local donors helped us **get** the after-school program **off the ground**.

drill.sentence: The idea for a neighborhood garden was great, but it took a whole year to {{get it off the ground}}.
drill.hint: make it start working (a flying image; not *going* or *started*)

entries.related: *get the ball rolling* — start an activity; *take off* — suddenly become successful; *never get off the ground* — fail at the very start.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make more effort than is expected or required, especially to help someone.
entries.usage: Positive and very common in customer service, reviews and praise for workers: *She always goes the extra mile for her students.* It is often followed by *for* + person or *to* + verb. Because it appears so often in job ads and references, it can sound like business language.
entries.pattern: go the extra mile (for someone / to + verb)
examples: The hotel staff **went the extra mile** and decorated our room for our anniversary.
Our pediatrician always **goes the extra mile**, even calling at night to check on the baby.
If you want the scholarship, you'll have to **go the extra mile** on your application essay.

drill.sentence: Our mechanic {{went the extra mile}} and drove the car to our house when the repair was done.
drill.hint: did more than was expected (not *above and beyond*)

entries.related: *go above and beyond* — same; *bend over backwards* — try very hard to help, sometimes too hard; *do the bare minimum* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To work or study until very late at night.
entries.usage: Usually about students before exams or workers before deadlines, often in the progressive: *I've been burning the midnight oil all week.* It is neutral and a little old-fashioned. It suggests hard work, never partying.
examples: She's been **burning the midnight oil** all week to finish her taxes before the deadline.
Before finals, the library is full of students **burning the midnight oil**.
The wedding planner **burned the midnight oil** fixing the seating chart after three guests canceled.

drill.sentence: If you want to finish the kitchen before your in-laws arrive, you'll have to {{burn the midnight oil}}.
drill.hint: work late into the night (a lamp image; not *pull an all-nighter*)

entries.related: *pull an all-nighter* — stay up the whole night working or studying; *work late* — plainer; *get an early night* — go to bed early.
entries.origin: From the days when people worked at night by the light of oil lamps.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To suddenly become too nervous or afraid to do something you had planned, such as getting married or making a big decision.
entries.usage: Informal and especially common about weddings, but also about deals, trips and big purchases: *He got cold feet the night before the wedding.* It usually takes *get* or *have*. It suggests a loss of courage, not a change of mind for good reasons.
entries.pattern: get / have cold feet (about + plan)
examples: Two days before the wedding, the groom **got cold feet** and called it off.
We were ready to buy the house, but my husband **got cold feet** when he saw the mortgage numbers.
She signed up for skydiving but **got cold feet** in the parking lot.

drill.sentence: He was all set to quit his job and travel for a year, but he {{got cold feet}} at the last minute.
drill.hint: became too nervous to go ahead (not *chickened out* or *had second thoughts*)

entries.related: *chicken out* — informal, decide not to do something because of fear; *have second thoughts* — start to doubt a decision; *take the plunge* — the opposite, finally do something risky.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To help someone, especially with a practical or physical task.
entries.usage: Informal and very common in requests and offers: *Can you give me a hand with these boxes?* The task follows *with* + noun or *-ing*. Note that *give someone a big hand* means applaud them, so context matters.
entries.pattern: give someone a hand (with + noun / -ing)
examples: Could you **give me a hand** with these grocery bags? My arms are full.
Our neighbor **gave us a hand** moving the couch up to the third floor.
If you finish early, go **give** your sister **a hand** in the kitchen.

drill.sentence: This table is heavier than it looks — can you {{give me a hand}} carrying it outside?
drill.hint: offer some practical help (the verb is not *lend*)

entries.related: *lend a hand* — same; *give someone a big hand* — applaud them; *pitch in* — join others to help.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In trouble, usually with someone in authority, because of something you did.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation and news: *He's in hot water with his boss.* Typical verbs are *be, get, find yourself* and *land*, often with *with* + person or *over* / *for* + reason. It suggests serious trouble, but not a disaster.
entries.pattern: be / get / land in hot water (with someone) (over / for + something)
examples: My brother is **in hot water** with my mom for denting her car.
The restaurant landed **in hot water** after a health inspector found mice in the kitchen.
You'll be **in hot water** with your manager if you miss another deadline.

drill.sentence: The coach found himself {{in hot water}} after he was caught yelling at a referee in the parking lot.
drill.hint: facing trouble because of his actions (not *in trouble*)

entries.related: *in trouble* — plainer; *in the doghouse* — informal, in trouble with a partner or family; *off the hook* — the opposite, out of trouble.

entries.term: let the cat out of the bag
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To reveal a secret, usually by accident.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, especially about surprises, gifts, pregnancies and plans: *Who let the cat out of the bag?* It suggests a careless slip rather than a deliberate betrayal. The past form is *let*.
examples: We were planning a surprise party, but my son **let the cat out of the bag** at breakfast.
The company **let the cat out of the bag** when it accidentally posted photos of the new phone on its website.
Don't tell Grandpa about the baby yet — he'll **let the cat out of the bag** to the whole family.

drill.sentence: I wasn't supposed to say anything about her engagement, but I {{let the cat out of the bag}} at lunch.
drill.hint: revealed the secret by accident (an animal image; not *spilled the beans*)

entries.related: *spill the beans* — tell secret information, often on purpose; *give the game away* — reveal a plan or secret; *keep something under wraps* — the opposite, keep it secret.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To tell people secret or private information, often before you are supposed to.
entries.usage: Informal and playful; it can be on purpose or by accident, and *about* + topic often follows. It is a common invitation to share gossip or news: *Come on, spill the beans!* *Spill!* on its own is a slang version.
entries.pattern: spill the beans (about + something)
examples: Come on, **spill the beans** — how did the date go?
One of the actors **spilled the beans** about the ending in a podcast interview.
My mom made me promise not to **spill the beans** about Dad's retirement party.

drill.sentence: The kids were supposed to keep our trip to Disney World a secret, but my youngest {{spilled the beans}} within an hour.
drill.hint: gave away the surprise (a food image; not *let the cat out*)

entries.related: *let the cat out of the bag* — reveal a secret, usually by mistake; *blab* — informal, talk too much and reveal secrets; *keep your mouth shut* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To lose an opportunity because you acted too slowly.
entries.usage: Informal; common about investments, jobs, deals, tickets and trends. It often appears as *have missed the boat* or *miss the boat on* + something. *Miss out* is similar but does not stress being too late.
entries.pattern: miss the boat (on + something)
examples: I thought about buying a house in that neighborhood ten years ago, but I **missed the boat**; now prices are crazy.
The store **missed the boat** on online ordering and lost half its customers.
Tickets sold out in an hour, so anyone who waited until the evening **missed the boat**.

drill.sentence: The early-bird discount ended yesterday, so I'm afraid you've {{missed the boat}}.
drill.hint: lost your chance by waiting too long (a water-travel image; not *… out*)

entries.related: *miss out (on something)* — not get a chance to do something enjoyable; *too little, too late* — action that comes after it could help; *jump on the bandwagon* — join something popular.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very rarely; almost never.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation about habits and rare events: *I only eat fast food once in a blue moon.* It usually goes at the end of the clause, often after *only*. It sounds light and a little humorous.
examples: My brother lives in Alaska, so we only see him **once in a blue moon**.
I drink soda **once in a blue moon**, usually at baseball games.
**Once in a blue moon**, the buses in this city actually run on time.

drill.sentence: My dad hates restaurants, so we only eat out {{once in a blue moon}}.
drill.hint: almost never (a night-sky image)

entries.related: *every now and then* — sometimes, not often; *hardly ever* — almost never, plainer; *all the time* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To avoid risks and choose the careful option.
entries.usage: Neutral and very common in advice and decisions: *I'll play it safe and leave early.* It is often followed by *and* + verb or *by* + *-ing*. It can be neutral or mildly critical, when someone is too cautious to do anything interesting.
entries.pattern: play it safe (and + verb / by + -ing)
examples: The forecast said it might snow, so we **played it safe** and left for the airport three hours early.
The band **played it safe** on their new album, and some fans called it boring.
I'm not sure if the chicken is still good, so let's **play it safe** and order takeout.

drill.sentence: I wasn't sure about the dress code, so I {{played it safe}} and wore a suit.
drill.hint: chose the careful option (not *erred on the side of caution*)

entries.related: *err on the side of caution* — choose the safer option, more formal; *take a chance* — the opposite; *better safe than sorry* — a saying used to defend careful choices.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To sound familiar, although you cannot remember exactly why or where you heard it.
entries.usage: Informal and very common with names, places and words, often in questions and in the negative: *Does the name Kevin Walsh ring a bell?* *It doesn't ring a bell.* The subject is the name or thing, not the person who remembers.
entries.pattern: X rings a bell; does X ring a bell (with you)?
examples: Her name **rings a bell**, but I can't remember where we met.
Does the name Kevin Walsh **ring a bell**? He says he went to high school with you.
I've heard this song before — the melody definitely **rings a bell**.

drill.sentence: The address on the envelope {{rang a bell}}, and then I remembered: it was my first apartment.
drill.hint: was somehow familiar (a sound image; not *looked familiar*)

mistake.wrong: That name rings me a bell.
mistake.why: *Ring a bell* takes no personal object; if you need the person, say *rings a bell with me*.

entries.related: *sound familiar* — plainer; *jog someone's memory* — help someone remember; *draw a blank* — the opposite, remember nothing.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The advantages of two different things or situations at the same time, without their usual disadvantages.
entries.usage: Positive and common in conversation and advertising: *With a hybrid job, you get the best of both worlds.* It usually follows *get, have, enjoy, offer* or *be*. It describes a choice that avoids the usual trade-off.
entries.pattern: get / have / offer the best of both worlds
examples: Living in a small town near a big city gives us **the best of both worlds**.
Working from home three days a week is **the best of both worlds**: quiet time and real coworkers.
This restaurant offers **the best of both worlds** — a fancy menu at diner prices.

drill.sentence: Our cabin is ten minutes from the ski slopes and twenty from the beach, so we get {{the best of both worlds}}.
drill.hint: the advantages of two different things at once

entries.related: *have your cake and eat it too* — want two things that cannot go together; *a win-win* — good for everyone involved; *a trade-off* — the opposite idea, giving up one thing to get another.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Time seems to pass very quickly, often more quickly than you had noticed.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, usually as a short remark when you realize how much time has passed: *Wow, time flies!* *Time flies when you're having fun* is the full saying, often used ironically about boring things. It is usually in the simple present, but *time flew* and *the week flew by* are also common.
examples: My little girl starts college next week — **time flies**.
We've been married ten years already? Wow, **time flies**.
**Time flies** when you're having fun; I can't believe the vacation is already over.

drill.sentence: Has it really been five years since we graduated? {{Time flies}}!
drill.hint: the years go by so fast — a two-word saying

entries.related: *time flies when you're having fun* — the full saying; *where did the time go?* — said when you're surprised how fast time passed; *time drags* — the opposite, time passes slowly.
entries.origin: From the Latin saying *tempus fugit*, *time flees*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An idea or piece of information that makes you think seriously about something.
entries.usage: Neutral; common after talks, articles and conversations: *That gave me food for thought.* It is usually the object of *give* or *provide*, or follows *That's*. It is uncountable: *some food for thought*, never *a food for thought*.
entries.pattern: give someone / provide food for thought; that's food for thought
examples: The speaker's point about screen time gave a lot of parents **food for thought**.
Thanks for the advice about changing careers — that's real **food for thought**.
The documentary about fast fashion left me with some **food for thought** about my closet.

drill.sentence: Her question about why I really want to move abroad gave me {{food for thought}}.
drill.hint: an idea to consider carefully (a meal image; not *something to chew on*)

entries.related: *something to chew on* — informal, same; *a wake-up call* — an event that makes you realize a problem; *give someone pause* — make someone stop and think.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To understand a meaning or feeling that is hinted at but not stated directly.
entries.usage: Neutral and common about messages, emails, statements and conversations, often with *you have to* or *if you*: *If you read between the lines, he's unhappy.* It suggests close attention to tone and to what is left out.
examples: Her text just said she was fine, but **reading between the lines**, I think she's upset.
If you **read between the lines** of the company's statement, they're planning layoffs.
Kids are good at **reading between the lines** when their parents say everything is OK.

drill.sentence: Grandpa keeps saying he's doing fine on his own, but it's not hard to {{read between the lines}}: he's lonely.
drill.hint: see the hidden meaning (a text image)

entries.related: *get the hint* — understand what someone suggests indirectly; *take something at face value* — the opposite, accept it as it seems; *subtext* — the hidden meaning.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In very few words; as a short summary.
entries.usage: Neutral and common in speech and informal writing to introduce or end a summary. It usually goes at the start of the sentence, followed by a comma (*In a nutshell, we need more time*), or at the end: *That's it in a nutshell.*
examples: **In a nutshell**, the car needs new brakes, new tires and a new battery.
So that's our story **in a nutshell**: we met at a bus stop and got married a year later.
Here's the new e-scooter law **in a nutshell**: no riding on sidewalks, and helmets for anyone under eighteen.

drill.sentence: I don't have time for the whole story — just tell me {{in a nutshell}} why you quit.
drill.hint: using very few words (not *in short* or *briefly*)

entries.related: *in short* — same, a bit more formal; *long story short* — informal, used to skip details; *in detail* — the opposite.

entries.term: on the tip of your tongue
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Almost remembered: you know a word or name but cannot quite say it at the moment.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about names, words and titles: *It's on the tip of my tongue!* The subject is the word or name you are trying to remember. The possessive changes with the person (*my, his, her*).
entries.pattern: it's (right) on the tip of my tongue
examples: The actor's name is **on the tip of my tongue** — he was in that movie about the submarine.
She had the answer **on the tip of her tongue**, but the buzzer went off first.
What's the word for a fear of small spaces? It's right **on the tip of my tongue**.

drill.sentence: What's the name of that Italian place we went to last summer? It's {{on the tip of my tongue}}.
drill.hint: almost there in my memory, but I can't say it

entries.related: *slip your mind* — be forgotten; *ring a bell* — sound familiar; *draw a blank* — be unable to remember anything at all.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To react quickly and well to a new situation, without time to prepare.
entries.usage: Usually praise; common in job ads, interviews and talk about teachers, nurses, lawyers and performers. It often follows *able to*, *have to* or *good at*. The possessive changes with the person (*think on her feet*).
entries.pattern: be able to / have to / be good at + thinking on your feet
examples: When the projector died, the speaker had to **think on her feet** and give the talk without slides.
Good ER nurses can **think on their feet** when three patients arrive at once.
My son is great at **thinking on his feet**; he can talk his way out of almost anything.

drill.sentence: When the bride's dress ripped right before the ceremony, the photographer had to {{think on his feet}} and fix it with tape.
drill.hint: react quickly without preparing (not *improvise* or *wing it*)

entries.related: *improvise* — make something up on the spot; *wing it* — informal, do something without preparation; *be caught off guard* — be surprised and not ready.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To start dealing seriously with the main task or topic, after preparations or small talk.
entries.usage: Common at the start of meetings and work sessions: *OK, let's get down to business.* It usually comes after chatting, introductions or coffee. It is neutral and friendly, though it signals that the relaxed part is over.
examples: After ten minutes of small talk about the weather, the lawyer finally **got down to business**.
OK, everyone's here, so let's **get down to business**: who's bringing what to the reunion?
The kids played for an hour before they **got down to business** and started their homework.

drill.sentence: Enough chatting about the game — we have a lot to cover, so let's {{get down to business}}.
drill.hint: start the serious work (not *get to work* or *get started*)

entries.related: *get to the point* — say the important thing directly; *get the ball rolling* — start an activity; *make small talk* — chat about unimportant things.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be very busy with work or responsibilities, so that you have no time for anything else.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often as a polite excuse or as sympathy: *She has her hands full with three kids.* The cause usually follows *with*. The possessive changes with the person.
entries.pattern: have your hands full (with + something)
examples: With twin babies and a full-time job, my sister really **has her hands full**.
Sorry I can't help this weekend — I **have my hands full** with the move.
The new coach **has his hands full**: the team lost its two best players over the summer.

drill.sentence: Don't ask Dad to fix the bike today; he {{has his hands full}} with the leaking roof.
drill.hint: is extremely busy (not *is swamped* or *is tied up*)

entries.related: *be swamped* — have too much to do; *be tied up* — be busy and not available; *have time on your hands* — the opposite, have free time.

entries.term: have your work cut out for you
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To face a very difficult task that will need a lot of effort.
entries.usage: Common in sports, work and news, often about someone starting a hard job: *The new manager has her work cut out for her.* The form with *for you* is the usual American one; British speakers often stop at *cut out*. The possessive and the pronoun change together (*they have their work cut out for them*).
entries.pattern: have your work cut out for you
examples: The new principal **has her work cut out for her** — the school has had four principals in five years.
If you want to run a marathon in two months, you **have your work cut out for you**.
Facing the champions in the first round, the Eagles **have their work cut out for them**.

drill.sentence: Our house hasn't been painted in thirty years, so whoever buys it will {{have their work cut out for them}}.
drill.hint: face a really hard job (not *have their hands full*)

entries.related: *a tall order* — a very difficult task; *have your hands full* — be very busy; *an uphill battle* — a long struggle against difficulties.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A very annoying person, thing or task.
entries.usage: Informal but polite enough for most conversations: *Filling out these forms is a pain in the neck.* It usually follows *be* or comes in *What a pain in the neck!* *A pain in the butt* is ruder, and *a pain* on its own is also common.
examples: Parking downtown is **a pain in the neck**, so I usually take the train.
My little brother was **a pain in the neck** when we were kids, but now he's my best friend.
Changing your password every month is **a pain in the neck**, but it's company policy.

drill.sentence: Putting together that bookshelf was {{a pain in the neck}}; the instructions made no sense at all.
drill.hint: really annoying (not *a hassle* or *a headache*)

entries.related: *a hassle* — something annoying and inconvenient; *a headache* — a difficult problem; *a pain* — shorter, informal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make someone extremely annoyed, often by doing something again and again.
entries.usage: Informal and common in complaints about people, noises and habits: *His humming drives me up the wall.* The person goes after *drive*, and the subject is often a habit or a noise. *Drive someone crazy* and *drive someone nuts* are similar.
entries.pattern: something / someone drives someone up the wall
examples: My roommate's habit of leaving dirty dishes in the sink **drives me up the wall**.
The car alarm across the street went off all night and **drove** the whole block **up the wall**.
Kids asking if we're there yet every five minutes can **drive** any parent **up the wall**.

drill.sentence: The neighbor's dog barks every time a car goes by, and it's {{driving me up the wall}}.
drill.hint: making me extremely annoyed (not *crazy*, *nuts* or *on my nerves*)

entries.related: *drive someone crazy / nuts* — same; *get on someone's nerves* — annoy someone, a bit milder; *get under someone's skin* — annoy someone deeply.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To annoy or irritate someone, usually again and again over a period of time.
entries.usage: Informal and very common: *His jokes are starting to get on my nerves.* The subject is a person, a habit or a noise, and the possessive changes (*my, her, everyone's*). It is a little milder than *drive someone up the wall*, and often comes with *start to* or *really*.
entries.pattern: something / someone gets on someone's nerves
examples: I love my sister, but after a week in a tiny cabin, she started to **get on my nerves**.
That song is everywhere, and it's really **getting on my nerves**.
His constant phone calls during dinner **got on everyone's nerves**.

drill.sentence: My husband hums while he reads, and it's starting to {{get on my nerves}}.
drill.hint: irritate me (not *bug me*, *get to me* or *drive me crazy*)

entries.related: *drive someone up the wall* — stronger; *bug someone* — informal, annoy; *get under someone's skin* — annoy someone deeply.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Nervous, tense and easily upset, usually because you are worried about something.
entries.usage: Neutral and common in conversation and news about stress, danger or waiting for news: *Everyone's on edge before the results.* Typical verbs are *be, feel* and *put* or *keep someone*. It often describes a whole group: *The whole town is on edge.*
entries.pattern: be / feel on edge; put / keep someone on edge
examples: I've been **on edge** all day waiting for the doctor to call with my results.
After the break-ins, everyone on our street is a little **on edge**.
Too much coffee always puts me **on edge**.

drill.sentence: The players were clearly {{on edge}} before the final, snapping at reporters and at each other.
drill.hint: nervous and tense (two words; not *keyed up*)

entries.related: *on pins and needles* — anxiously waiting for news; *jumpy* — easily frightened; *at ease* — the opposite, relaxed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To hope that something will happen the way you want, or to wish someone good luck.
entries.usage: Informal and very common: *Keep your fingers crossed for me!* People often just say *Fingers crossed!*, and some actually cross two fingers as they say it. It is followed by *for* + person or a *that* clause.
entries.pattern: keep your fingers crossed (for someone / that …)
examples: My interview is at ten tomorrow, so **keep your fingers crossed** for me.
We're **keeping our fingers crossed** that the rain stops before the wedding.
The doctors are hopeful, and the whole family is **keeping their fingers crossed**.

drill.sentence: The adoption agency will call us next week, and we're {{keeping our fingers crossed}}.
drill.hint: hoping for good news (a hand gesture)

entries.related: *knock on wood* — said after something positive, to avoid bad luck; *hope for the best* — hope things go well; *break a leg* — good luck, said to performers.

entries.term: have a soft spot for someone
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To feel special affection for someone or something, often more than you can easily explain.
entries.usage: Warm and common about people, animals, places and foods: *I've always had a soft spot for old dogs.* It is followed by *for* + noun, often with *always*. It suggests you are kinder or less critical toward this person or thing than toward others.
entries.pattern: have (always had) a soft spot for + someone / something
examples: My grandmother always **had a soft spot for** my little brother, and everyone knew it.
I **have a soft spot for** cheesy 1980s movies, even the really bad ones.
The teacher **had a soft spot for** the quiet kids who sat in the back.

drill.sentence: Our neighbor acts grumpy, but he's always {{had a soft spot for}} stray cats.
drill.hint: felt special affection for (not *a weakness for*)

entries.related: *have a weakness for* — find something hard to resist; *be fond of* — like, more general; *can't stand* — the opposite, hate.

entries.term: wear your heart on your sleeve
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To show your feelings openly, so that other people can easily see them.
entries.usage: Used to describe someone's personality, usually kindly, but sometimes to suggest that they get hurt easily: *He wears his heart on his sleeve.* Both possessives change with the person (*she wears her heart on her sleeve*). It is usually in the simple present.
examples: My dad **wears his heart on his sleeve**; he cries at every wedding and graduation.
She **wears her heart on her sleeve**, so you always know when she's upset.
Fans love the coach because he **wears his heart on his sleeve** on the sidelines.

drill.sentence: Maya {{wears her heart on her sleeve}}, so it was obvious to everyone that the breakup hurt her.
drill.hint: shows her feelings openly (a clothing image)

entries.related: *an open book* — a person whose thoughts are easy to know; *keep a stiff upper lip* — hide your feelings, a British image; *poker-faced* — the opposite, showing no emotion.
entries.origin: An early well-known use is in Shakespeare's *Othello* (around 1603).

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Not the kind of thing you like or enjoy.
entries.usage: Informal and polite; a soft way to say you don't like something without criticizing it: *Opera isn't really my cup of tea.* It is almost always negative, and the possessive changes (*not his cup of tea*, *not everyone's cup of tea*). The subject is the activity or thing, not the person.
entries.pattern: X is not (really) my / his / everyone's cup of tea
examples: Camping in the rain isn't really **my cup of tea**, but the kids loved it.
I know reality TV is **not everyone's cup of tea**, but I can't stop watching it.
Big parties were never **his cup of tea**; he preferred dinner with a few close friends.

drill.sentence: Thanks for the invitation, but horror movies just aren't {{my cup of tea}}.
drill.hint: the kind of thing I enjoy (a drink image; not *my thing*)

entries.related: *not my thing* — informal, same; *not my scene* — not the kind of place or activity I like; *right up my alley* — the opposite, exactly what I like.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make someone very happy, usually with a small, unexpected act or piece of news.
entries.usage: Informal and warm; very common as thanks: *Your message made my day!* The possessive changes (*made her day*). *Go ahead, make my day*, a famous movie line, is used as a tough, ironic challenge.
examples: A stranger paid for my coffee this morning, and it totally **made my day**.
Your letter **made Grandma's day**; she read it to everyone at dinner.
When the team visited the children's hospital, the players really **made** the kids' **day**.

drill.sentence: My son called just to say he loved me, and it {{made my day}}.
drill.hint: put me in a great mood (not *brightened*)

entries.related: *brighten someone's day* — similar, a little milder; *make someone's week* — even stronger, informal; *ruin someone's day* — the opposite.
